Does the use of the name \"Coruna\" by the city of Coruna constitute trademark infringement under the Lanham Act?\n2. Does the use of the name \"Coruna\" by the city of Coruna dilute the distinctiveness of the Corona trademark under the Lanham Act?\n\nAnalysis:\n\n1. Trademark Infringement:\n\nTo establish trademark infringement under the Lanham Act, Corona must prove that (1) it has a valid and legally protectable trademark, and (2) the defendant's use of the mark is likely to cause confusion among consumers.\n\nCorona has a valid and legally protectable trademark, as evidenced by its registration in numerous countries. However, the likelihood of confusion analysis is more complex. Courts consider several factors when determining whether a defendant's use of a mark is likely to cause confusion, including the similarity of the marks, the similarity of the goods or services offered, the strength of the plaintiff's mark, the defendant's intent, and evidence of actual confusion.\n\nIn this case, the marks are similar in sound and appearance, which weighs in favor of a finding of likelihood of confusion. However, the goods and services offered by the parties are not similar, as Corona is a beer brand, and the city of Coruna is a municipality. This factor weighs against a finding of likelihood of confusion.\n\nThe strength of the Corona trademark is high, as it is a well-known and widely recognized brand. However, the defendant's intent is not to trade on the goodwill of the Corona brand, as the city of Coruna has used its name for centuries. Additionally, there is no evidence of actual confusion between the two marks.\n\nBased on these factors, it is unlikely that Corona will be able to establish trademark infringement under the Lanham Act.\n\n2. Additionally, there is no evidence of actual dilution of the Corona mark.\n\nBased on these factors, it is unlikely that Corona will be able to establish trademark dilution under the Lanham Act.\n\nConclusion:\n\nIn the hypothetical case of Corona v.
